name: Diorama
tagline: A browser based tool for dressing up product screenshots into polished marketing visuals: device frames, backgrounds, shadows, annotations.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The core mechanic here is compositing: take an image, put it on a nicer background, add a frame, a shadow, maybe a caption, export at 2x. That is a canvas, a few CSS transforms and a PNG export, and an agent will get you a working version in a sitting. What you will not get in one shot is the taste: the preset gradients, the device bezels that look right, the shadow falloff that does not scream amateur, the export sizes that match every app store and social card spec. You also lose browser capture, team presets and the slow accumulation of templates that make the paid tool fast instead of fiddly. Fine if you ship two screenshots a month, annoying if screenshots are your job.
coreLoopDIY: Drop in a screenshot, pick a background and a device frame, nudge position and rotation, export a high resolution PNG at a chosen preset size.
requirements: Node and npm for local dev
Optional: device bezel PNGs you source or draw yourself
whatYouLose: Hand tuned presets and bezels that actually look professional
Export presets matched to app store and social dimensions you did not know existed
Any in browser or URL capture step, you bring your own screenshots
Shared templates and brand kits for a team
Someone else maintaining the 3D perspective math when it looks subtly wrong
moatNotes: The moat is pixel taste, not technology. Nothing here is hard; looking good is.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the gap between a screenshot on a gradient and a screenshot that looks like a funded company shipped it is entirely in details you will not enjoy tuning: bezel curvature, shadow spread, perspective skew, retina export. A paid tool hands you fifty defaults made by someone with an eye. A self-built one hands you a slider and a vague sense that something is off.
notes: Weekend project with a long taste tail: the build is easy, the presets are the product.
prompt:
Build a local, single page screenshot beautifier web app. No accounts, no backend, no telemetry, no cloud uploads. Everything runs in the browser.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Vite + React + TypeScript
- Tailwind CSS for UI
- HTML canvas for rendering and export
- Zustand for state
- No server, no database, no auth

Core flow:
1. User drags an image file onto the page or pastes from clipboard.
2. The image renders centered on a background inside a live preview canvas.
3. A right side panel controls: background (solid color, linear gradient with two color pickers and angle, or transparent), padding, corner radius on the screenshot, shadow (blur, opacity, y offset), rotation, scale, and optional 3D tilt using CSS style perspective math applied on canvas.
4. A frame dropdown: none, plain border, browser chrome bar with three fake traffic light dots and an editable URL text, generic phone bezel drawn with rounded rects (do not ship copyrighted device art).
5. An annotation layer: click to add a text label or an arrow, drag to move, delete with backspace. Keep it simple, no rich text.
6. Export presets: original, 2x, 1200x630 OG, 1280x800, 1080x1080. Export writes a PNG via canvas.toBlob and triggers a download.

Also required:
- Persist the last used settings in localStorage so reopening keeps the look.
- Save and load named presets as JSON, stored in localStorage, with export and import buttons.
- Ship at least eight decent built in gradient backgrounds defined in a single file so they are easy to edit.
- Keyboard: cmd+v paste image, cmd+s export.

Explicitly out of scope: capturing screenshots or URLs, video, team sharing, any network call, any analytics.

Deliver a README with npm install and npm run dev, a .env.example only if you genuinely need a secret (you should not), and keep the whole thing under roughly 1200 lines of readable code.
